title: How to Evaluate a Trust and Safety Vendor: 25 Questions to Ask Before You Sign
summary: A buyer's checklist for trust and safety vendor evaluation: decision quality, policy fit, human review, compliance, pricing, and how to test a vendor in shadow mode before cutover.
body_markdown:
Most trust and safety vendor decisions are made on a demo and a price sheet. Six months later the team finds out the vendor's classifier does not know where their policies draw the line, escalation takes two days, and nobody can explain why a decision went the way it did.


This guide helps you evaluate a vendor with more precision and sophistication. It covers what to ask, what evidence to demand, and how to test a vendor against your own queue before you commit.


## **1. Decision quality on your policies**


A headline accuracy number shows how a system performs on a standard test set. For your decision, you also need to know how it performs against your own policy definitions.


Ask:


• How is accuracy measured, on what data, and against whose labels?


• Can the system be configured to your written policies, including exceptions and edge cases?


• What are precision and recall for each harm type you care about, reported separately?


• What is the false positive rate on benign content that looks risky (reclaimed language, news reporting, gaming banter, satire)?


• How does the system handle context such as prior messages, user history, or surrounding content?


• Which harm types does the vendor automate today, and which does it route to humans? Be wary of any vendor that claims full autonomy across every harm type.


**What good looks like:** per-policy metrics, your labeled ground truth used as the test set, and a clear statement of where automation stops and review starts.


## **2. Speed and throughput**


• What is median and p95 turnaround for automated decisions? For escalated decisions?


• How does latency change at peak volume or during a spike in abuse?


• What are the SLAs, and what happens when they are missed?


## **3. Human review and escalation**


Automation clears the clear cases. Hard calls still need people, and the handoff is where many deployments break down.


• Which decisions escalate, and who sets the thresholds?


• Can your own reviewers work in the same tool, or are you buying outsourced reviewers only?


• How are reviewer decisions fed back to improve automated decisions?


• How do appeals and case management work, and are they in the same system as the original decision?


• What QA runs on review quality, and can you see it?


## **4. Auditability and governance**


• Can you see why each decision was made, which policy it mapped to, and what signals were used?


• Is there a full audit trail for every decision, change in policy, and change in threshold?


• Can you export decisions and evidence for regulators or internal audit?


• Who can change policies and workflows, and how are changes tested before they go live?


A single system for policies, workflows, human review, automated decisions, audits, and analytics gives you answers to these questions.


## **5. Security, privacy, and compliance**


• Which certifications does the vendor hold (for example SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001), and can you see the reports?


• Where is data stored and processed, and how long is it retained?


• Is your data used to train models for other customers?


• How does the vendor support your obligations under regulations such as the EU Digital Services Act and the UK Online Safety Act?


Bring legal and data protection into the process early. Enterprise deals stall most often when this review starts after the technical evaluation.


## **6. Pricing and total cost**


• What is the pricing unit (per item, per decision, per seat, per review), and what does it cost at 2x your current volume?


• What is excluded: integrations, policy tuning, reviewer hours, new harm types?


• What does migration off the vendor look like?


## **A simple scorecard**


Criterion Weight What to measure Evidence to request


Decision quality 30% Precision and recall per policy, false positive rate Results on your labeled sample


Speed 15% Median and p95 turnaround Live shadow-mode timings


Human review and escalation 20% Escalation accuracy, reviewer tooling, feedback loop Walkthrough in your queue


Auditability 15% Decision explanations, audit trail, exports Sample audit export


Security and compliance 10% Certifications, data handling Reports and DPA


Cost at scale 10% Total cost at current and 2x volume Written quote


Adjust the weights to your risk profile. A child safety team will weight decision quality and escalation higher than cost. A small team with a thin review bench may weight tooling and cost higher.


## **Test in shadow mode before you commit**


The most reliable evaluation runs the vendor in your live moderation queue alongside your incumbent, without taking action. You compare both systems against your own reviewers' decisions on the same content.


A workable plan:


• Define the test set. Pull a representative sample from your queue, including borderline cases and the harm types that hurt most.


• Fix ground truth. Have your reviewers label the sample against your current written policies.


• Run in parallel. Route live traffic to the vendor in shadow mode for two to four weeks.


• Score per policy. Compare accuracy, false positives, and turnaround against the incumbent and against ground truth.


• Review the disagreements. The cases where the vendor and your reviewers differ tell you the most about policy fit.


• Decide on evidence. Cut over only the policies where the vendor clears your threshold. Keep humans on the rest.


## **Red flags**


• Accuracy claims with no stated dataset or definition of "correct."


• No per-policy reporting.


• No way to see why a decision was made.


• A pilot that is a scripted demo rather than your own data.


• Pricing that cannot be modeled at your volume.


• A pitch that leads with headcount reduction rather than decision quality.


## FAQ


### What is the most important factor in choosing a trust and safety vendor?


Decision quality on your own policies, measured on your own labeled data. Everything else depends on it.


### How long should a vendor evaluation take?


A shadow-mode test typically needs two to four weeks of live traffic, plus time for legal and data protection review, which should start at the beginning.


### Should we use one vendor for AI and human review?


Ask whether the system lets your reviewers and automated decisions work in the same workflow with a shared audit trail. Fragmented tools make QA and appeals harder.


### How do we compare vendors fairly?


Use the same test set, the same ground truth, and the same scorecard for every vendor, and score each policy separately.
